This isn't a scene from a film. This is a heartbreaking reality that still exists in parts of Nepal. For some women and girls, getting their period means being sent away from their own home to spend the night in a small shed, away from their families. They are left to face cold nights, fear, loneliness, and the danger of snakes, insects, and wild animals—all because of a natural biological process. Menstruation should never be a reason for exclusion or shame. Take a moment and ask yourself: If it were someone you love—your daughter, your sister, your wife, or your mother—would you accept this as "tradition"? Some customs deserve to be questioned, especially when they put lives and dignity at risk. Every woman deserves to feel safe, respected, and valued, no matter what day of the month it is. Let's raise awareness, start conversations, and stand together to end harmful practices like this. Credit: insta/swachchhamahinabari Video: Dhani Rokaya (27) #NepalNow #EndChhaupadi #MenstrualHealth #PeriodDignity #WomensRights #SwachchhaMahinabari #Nepal

A suburban family is clinging to hope as they search for their loved one who went missing in the catastrophic flash floods in Nepal on Wednesday. Poonam Dilipkumar Thakkar, 42, left her home in Bartlett for Nepal last Thursday for a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity” to visit Mount Kailash. She traveled to the region as part of a religious pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which Hindus believe is the home of the god Shiva. Thakkar checked in with her family from Hotel Kailash in Timure where she was staying Wednesday morning. But the hotel is no longer standing, her family said. Shortly after Thakkar’s call home, massive flash floods swept through the border region between Nepal and China, wiping out communities and leaving thousands of people missing. Her family hasn’t heard from her since. They said they won’t give up until she is found. “We have hope that she will be found,” Thakkar's sister, Bhumika Sachdev, said. “She’s somewhere.” Read more at suntimes.com Story: Cindy Hernandez/Sun-Times Video: Courtesy of Thakkar's family

The road to Manang doesnt make promises. It tests you first. I came during the monsoon when the mountain roads turned into mud, the cliffs crumbled without warning and every bend carried the possibility of a landslide. In Nepal’s Himalayas, the journey can be just as unforgiving as the mountains themselves. But some places are worth the risk. Manang, deep inside the Annapurna Conservation Area is one of them. The jeep road ends here. Beyond this point theres only one way forward, on foot. This is where the legendary Annapurna Circuit truly begins. Depending on your pace, the trek takes around 12 days, carrying you through some of the most breathtaking landscapes on Earth. I came in the off season. Fewer people, quieter trails, raw weather. And somehow it made the experience feel even more real. Sometimes the hardest roads lead to the places you will never forget.♥️ #manang #nepal #traveltiktok #mountains #annapurna
